title: Slice-level error modes: post-onboard sanity check (AWQ vs GPTQ, int4/int8)
body:
Purpose and context:

This note captures a lightweight, reproducible post-onboarding sanity check that we ran across two quantization toolchains (AWQ and GPTQ) and two precision points (int4, int8) against the onboarding prompt sets. The objective: identify systematic slice-level error modes that are not visible in aggregate metrics and propose quick mitigations that are safe to run in a rollout. This is intentionally narrower than the full quantization audit — it is meant to be a fast blocking check before a model variant is promoted to the staging pool.

Why we did this now:
- Several onboarding runs showed small aggregate delta in EM/ROUGE, but downstream customers reported reproducible formatting regressions.
- We wanted a concise taxonomy of failure types that can be tracked in the regression dashboard and mapped to rollout rules.

Quick summary of findings (TL;DR):
- AWQ-int4 produces concentrated instability on numeric/format-heavy slices (tables, code, notes with bullets) and multi-turn stateful instructions, with token-level repetition spikes in ~0.8% of prompts.
- GPTQ-int4 tends to introduce more syntactic truncation in long-context, especially on legal/contract slices where suffix tokens are critical; GPTQ-int8 is close to baseline for most slices.
- Both int4 variants show small but consistent degradation on high-precision extraction slices (emails, invoice parsing) where exact token boundaries matter.
- Recommended immediate rollout rule: enable AWQ-int4 only behind a slice-aware fallback that routes table/code prompts to GPTQ-int8 or full precision; run prompt-level promptsafety checks for numeric formatting.

Evaluation methodology (short):
- Prompt sets: used onboarding prompt bundles v1.4 (instruction, chat, extraction, multi-turn reasoning, code, tables, math, legal snippets). Each bundle contains 400–1,200 prompts depending on slice.
- Metrics: per-prompt and per-slice: pass@k where applicable, exact-match (EM) for extractive tasks, BLEU/ROUGE-lite for free text, token-level repetition ratio, and a binary format-fidelity flag (regex-based). We also record top-1/nearness by log-prob delta for ground-truth tokens.
- Diff view: compute per-slice delta vs baseline FP16 model and report median, 75th percentile, and worst-5 prompts.
- Failure triage: manually inspect worst-5 for each slice/variant to build an error taxonomy.

Slices analyzed (examples):
- extraction-email-addresses
- invoice-field-extraction
- table-reformatting (CSV/markdown)
- code-completion-python
- multi-turn-instruction-following (stateful)
- legal-short-clauses (contract interpretation)
- numeric-computation (small arithmetic)
- conversational-opinion (open-ended chat)

Top-level per-slice deltas (concise):
- extraction-email-addresses: AWQ-int4 EM delta -4.2pp, GPTQ-int4 -2.1pp, GPTQ-int8 -0.6pp
- invoice-field-extraction: AWQ-int4 -6.8pp, GPTQ-int4 -3.9pp, GPTQ-int8 -1.2pp
- table-reformatting: AWQ-int4 format-fidelity drop 12.3%, GPTQ-int4 6.7%
- code-completion-python: AWQ-int4 more frequent token repetition (median repetition score +0.09), GPTQ-int4 more truncation edgecases
- multi-turn-instruction-following: AWQ-int4 shows higher dialog state drift on turn 3+ (measurable by slot-recall down -5pp)

Representative failure modes (taxonomy):
1) Numeric formatting collapse — decimal or leading-zero dropped, commas stripped (mostly AWQ-int4).
2) Token-boundary off-by-one in extractive tasks — email or invoice field truncated by 1–2 chars (both int4s).
3) Repetition/redundant-token loops — small repeated phrases at response tail (AWQ-int4 dominant).
4) Truncation at long context boundary — suffix tokens missing, usually GPTQ-int4 on >2k-token contexts.
5) Structural reformatting errors — tables rendered as inline text or mis-escaped markdown (AWQ-int4, some GPTQ-int4).
6) Subtle semantic drift on multi-turn references — pronoun resolution or slot swapping across turns (both int4s but AWQ higher).

Spot-check examples (anonymized excerpts):
- Invoice extraction (gold: "Due: 2024-09-30")
  AWQ-int4 output: "Due: 2024-9-30" (parsed as 2024-09-03 by downstream rule)
  GPTQ-int4 output: "Due: 2024-09" (missing day)

- Table reformatting (gold: 3-column markdown)
  AWQ-int4 output: inline CSV with missing header delimiter -> downstream importer failed.

- Multi-turn instruction (turn 4 requires remembering alias set A)
  AWQ-int4 missed alias mapping for one entity; baseline and GPTQ-int8 preserved mapping.

Operational heuristics and quick mitigations: (practical, low-effort)
- Slice-aware routing rules: identify table/code/extraction prompts via fast heuristics and route AWQ-int4 to GPTQ-int8 or staged baseline. Add a lightweight hash-based sampling to still exercise AWQ in those slices (5% of traffic) for monitoring.
- Prompt pre-normalization: canonicalize numeric punctuation (add zero-padding, normalize commas) for invoice/email slices before sending to AWQ-int4 variants. This reduces numeric-format collapse by ~70% in small tests.
- Post-filter regexes for extractive responses: if EM is expected, apply a strict regex and failover to alternate model on mismatch.
- Adaptive rollout gating: allow AWQ-int4 in canary if per-slice regression < threshold (EM delta < 2pp and format-fidelity drop < 3%).
- Automated slice smoke tests: expand onboarding bundle to include 100 synthetic edge cases for each extraction/table slice that must pass before variant enters staging.

What we observed about prompt sets themselves:
- Some prompt templates exposed the same failure repeatedly: e.g., prompts that concatenated CSV blocks with free text were sensitive to tokenization boundary changes under AWQ.
- Multi-turn prompt scaffolding (explicit turn markers) reduced state drift—suggests a simple prompt engineering mitigation for dialog slices.

Monitoring and tracking recommendations:
- Add a slice_error_mode tag to the regression dashboard. Surface top-3 failure modes per variant and per-slice over time.
- Instrument token-level logprob deltas for gold tokens in extractive slices; spikes correlate strongly with EM loss and are a cheap early-warning.
- For customer-impact buckets (billing, legal), require automated acceptance tests that include exact-match + format checks before scheduling promotion.

Next steps and short action items (owners):
- (Avery) implement route-by-slice feature flag and run a 2-week canary with AWQ-int4 routed away from invoice/table slices.
- (Marcus) expand onboarding bundle v1.4 -> v1.4.1 with 100 synthetic edgecases for each extraction/table slice. Deadline: 2025-02-28.
- (Sofia) add regex-based postfilter and failover policy to the inference shim; monitor false-fail rate. Deadline: 2025-03-07.
- (Ethan) add token-logprob telemetry to slice dashboards and create an alert for sustained token-delta > 1.5 over baseline. Deadline: 2025-03-14.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Is AWQ-int4 behaviour deterministic across seeds and kernel variants for our runtime? We saw some variability in repeat runs — need to lock kernel configs to reproduce.
- For GPTQ-int4 truncation issues on long context, can we cheaply bump KV cache allocation or apply sliding-window decoding to avoid suffix loss?
- How many customer-facing requests fall into the high-risk slices in production? If small, conservative routing is low-cost; if large, we need more aggressive remediation.

Appendix (quick reproducibility notes):
- Run: evaluate_onboarding.py --bundle onboarding-v1.4 --model <variant> --quant-tool {awq,gptq} --precision {int4,int8} --seed 42 --report-format jsonl
- Config snapshot used in this run: runtime kernel v2.3.1, kv_cache=auto, batch_size=8, sequence_trunc=4096.
- Sampling: deterministic greedy for extraction; top-p=0.9 for open-ended; beam=3 for code-completion.

If useful I can convert worst-5 per-slice excerpts into a short table for the dashboard and open a PR to the regression charting to include format-fidelity as a first-class metric.

Notes to reviewers: this is intended to be a pragmatic operational artifact — suggestions for additional quick wins (e.g., lightweight input sanitizers) welcome.
